Groups in Action

A Mexico City Gathering on Symmetry and Discrete Structures

Thursday 10 & Friday 11 September, 2026
Auditorio Nápoles Gándara
Instituto de Matemáticas, UNAM, Mexico City

About the meeting

Groups in Action is a two-day gathering on the interplay between group theory and discrete structures: graphs, maps, polytopes, and other combinatorial objects with a high degree of symmetry. Talks run Thursday afternoon and all day Friday.

Registration is now closed.

Program

Thursday 10 September · afternoon

15:00 – 15:50Steve Wilson
The Capuzzi Dichotomies
Abstract

The most beautiful structure I have encountered as a mathematician is the Capuzzi Dichotomies. This set of 14 partitions of the numbers from 1 to 8, each into two disjoint sets of size four, is, first of all, more symmetric than we would expect. We will see why.

Hidden deep within it are other symmetric structures and surprising connections to other objects of high symmetry.

I will show some of its secrets, show where it comes from and show two paths on the route of my so far fruitless quest to generalize it, and so find even greater mysteries and connections.

16:00 – 16:30Coffee break
16:30 – 17:10Philippe Tranchida
Operations on groups extended to geometries
Abstract

Coset geometries provide a natural way to study incidence structures through groups and their subgroups. In this talk, I will discuss how several familiar constructions from group theory can be extended to the setting of coset geometries.

I will begin with a concrete example coming from the halving operation on polytopes. We will then explore the case of amalgamated products and HNN-extensions. I will finish by describing how these ideas suggest a version of Bass–Serre theory for coset geometries.

17:15 – 17:55Pavol Kollár
Special subsets of automorphism groups of graphs
Abstract

Joint work with Tatiana Jajcayová and Primož Potočnik.

Consider a group G acting transitively on the set Ω of n elements. Transitivity in groups (thanks to standard theory) is characterised by “each element in Ω is mapped to every element in Ω precisely k times”. We generalise the above notion to arbitrary sets of permutations; an “r-regular family of permutations” F (defined already in [3] and also in [2] for the r = 1 case) is a set of permutations acting on Ω, such that “each element in Ω is mapped to every element in Ω precisely r times”. Specifically, we are interested in the question “given a transitive group G acting on Ω, what is the smallest F that is an r-regular family of permutations?”

To us, the case when G is the automorphism group of a given graph Γ, i.e. G = Aut(Γ), is of particular interest, where the ground work has been laid in the paper [3], where the authors introduce the deficiency indices, measuring “how Cayley-like” a given vertex-transitive graph is. Using the census of all vertex-transitive graphs from [1] we classify all deficiency values for small graphs.

[1] G. Royle, D. Holt, Vertex-transitive graphs on fewer than 48 vertices, J. Symbolic Comput. 101 (2020), 51–60.
[2] G. Gauyacq, On quasi-Cayley graphs, Discrete Appl. Math. 77 (1997), 43–58.
[3] R. Jajcay, G. A. Jones, r-regular families of graph automorphisms, European J. Combin. 79 (2019), 97–110.

Friday 11 September · all day

10:00 – 10:40Tatiana Jajcayová
Inverse Semigroups in Action
Abstract

In the first part of our talk, we will review some of the combinatorial methods used in inverse semigroup theory.

Inverse semigroups can be viewed as natural generalizations of groups: while every group can be represented via permutations (total one-to-one transformations), inverse semigroups can be represented via partial one-to-one transformations. We will introduce graphs (automata), called Schützenberger automata, that are related to presentations of inverse semigroups in a way similar to the way Cayley graphs are related to groups. As shown by the combinatorial approach introduced by Munn and extended by Stephen, these automata are instrumental in the study of structural and algorithmic questions concerning inverse semigroup presentations.

We will then consider actions of special groups on these graphs, which will allow us to employ the powerful Bass–Serre theory, and to consider structural questions concerning amalgams and HNN extensions of certain classes of inverse semigroups.

10:45 – 11:15Coffee break
11:15 – 11:55Micael Toledo
Highly symmetric unstable maniplexes
Joint work with Isabel Hubard.
12:00 – 12:40Dimitri Leemans
Testing chirality in incidence geometry
Abstract

Joint work with Wei-Juan Zhang.

In 1956, Jacques Tits developed the concept of an incidence geometry as an object generalizing the notion of incidence. He also established its close relation with groups and showed how to construct incidence geometries starting from a group and some of its subgroups, inventing the concept of a coset geometry. Specific classes of incidence geometries have been studied in various contexts. For instance, thin residually connected and regular incidence geometries with a linear diagram give the family of abstract regular polytopes, while thin residually connected and chiral incidence geometries with a linear diagram give the family of chiral polytopes.

In 2016, Maria Elisa Fernandes, Dimitri Leemans and Asia Weiss introduced the concept of hypertopes, that are thin and residually connected incidence geometries, as a generalization of abstract polytopes, dropping the linearity condition that is imposed on polytopes. They studied in particular two families of hypertopes, namely the regular ones (where the automorphism group has a unique orbit on the set of chambers) and the chiral ones (where the automorphism group has two orbits on the set of chambers with adjacent chambers in distinct orbits). They showed among other things that the automorphism group of a regular hypertope has to be a C-group and that the automorphism group of a chiral hypertope has to be a C+-group.

In the regular case, given a C-group, one can easily construct a coset geometry, and then results from Buekenhout, Hermand, Dehon and Leemans permit to translate the geometric properties of thinness, residual connectedness and flag-transitivity into group-theoretical properties. Such tests are available in the computational algebra software Magma. In the chiral case, we recently managed to translate these geometric properties into group-theoretical properties. This talk will describe the work we did in that direction.

13:00Lunch
15:00 – 15:40Elías Mochán
Vertex- and face-transitive polyhedra with trivial facet stabilizer
Abstract

While regular polyhedra are the most studied family of polyhedra, some other families have also been of interest. One popular family is that of semiregular polyhedra: those with regular faces and whose group acts transitively on their vertices. Monson and Schulte have some results on this kind of polyhedra, but they always assume that every automorphism of a face extends to an automorphism of the polyhedron. In this talk we construct examples with the opposite property: the only symmetry of a face that extends to the whole polyhedron is the identity. We will create such examples with the added condition of being face-transitive. We do this by applying certain voltage operations to regular and chiral polytopes of higher ranks.

15:45 – 16:25Robert Jajcay
Special truncations, their automorphism groups, and connections to topological graph theory
Abstract

Joint work with Jin-Xin Zhou.

While map truncations are among the better known techniques in topological graph theory, their use with respect to graphs is less studied, partially due to the fact that the truncation is not uniquely determined. This has been remedied by introducing the concept of neighborhood labeling, parallel to that of a rotary system used in topological graph theory, and later expanded to generalized truncations allowing for truncation by arbitrary graphs, not just cycles.

The majority of truncations are not particularly symmetric; however, a specific construction starting from arc-transitive graphs, called special generalized truncation via cycles, always produces vertex-transitive graphs. Classification of special generalized truncations via cycles of complete graphs has been completed by Wang, Yin and Zhou using group-theoretical techniques. In our presentation we shall revisit their result from the point of view of highly symmetric maps, and extend their results to special generalized truncations of complete bipartite graphs.

16:30 – 17:00Coffee break
17:00 – 17:40Eugenia O'Reilly
Flag-transitive, point-primitive biplanes and a special class of digraphs
Abstract

Joint work with Patricio Ricardo García-Vázquez and Briseida Trejo Escamilla.

Biplanes are \((v,k,2)\)-symmetric designs. Those that admit a flag-transitive and point-primitive automorphism group have been shown to be of almost simple or affine type. The almost simple case has been exhaustively classified. In the affine case \(v\) must be a prime power \(q=p^r\), and in the only remaining open instance, which is when the automorphism group is contained in the group of semilinear transformations of a one-dimensional vector space over the field with \(q\) elements, we know \(q\) must be odd (here the set of points must be \(\mathbb{F}_q\)). A \((v,k,\lambda)\)-difference set in an additive abelian group \(G\) is a \(k\)-subset \(S\) of \(G\) such that the multiset of non-zero differences of elements in \(S\) contains each non-zero element of \(G\) exactly \(\lambda\) times. It has been shown by Biliotti and Montinaro [1] that if \(D\) is a flag-transitive, point-primitive \((v,k,\lambda)\)-symmetric design with \((k,\lambda)=1\) admitting an automorphism group of affine type \(G\), then \(G\leq A\Gamma L_1(q)\) and the blocks are the translates of a \((v,k,\lambda)\)-difference set in \(G\). Given this structure, we used the classical presentation by Foulser which allowed a computer search that determines there is no flag-transitive, point-primitive biplane with \(37

If I still have time, I will show how the condition that in a difference set all non-zero differences must appear exactly the same number of times (\(\lambda\)) can be relaxed so that, given an additive abelian group \(G\) of order \(v\) and a \(k\)-subset \(S\) of \(G\), the number of times each non-zero difference of elements of \(S\) appears can be one of a few different values, and this value only depends on which coset of \(S\) such a difference is found in. There is some balance here, and inspired by graceful graphs the difference digraphs were defined.

[1] M. Biliotti, A. Montinaro, On flag-transitive symmetric designs of affine type, J. Combin. Designs 25 (2017), 85–97.
